accuracy.reason: All eight objectives accurately scope database authority, application-owned cache-aside, complete keys, stale refill after invalidation, TTL versus eviction, independent/shared copies, bounded fallback and workload-led value. Sources and diagrams support these distinctions; no freshness or outage-safety guarantee.

evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.

mechanisms.reason: Hit/miss diagrams name the application actions; price update and delayed reader trace the stale-refill race. Coalescing shares one source operation, while capped fallback controls outage load. TTL and local/shared loss scenarios are causally explained well enough for learner transfer to distinct examples.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same key together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

coherence.reason: Reuse benefit leads to flow, ownership/key, updates, disappearance, placement and load failure, then decision. All prerequisites and eight objectives are connected. The stale-price diagram shows pre-invalidation state and prose separately explains why invalidation is insufficient.

evidence.quote: The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the result from the database on its own.

decisions.reason: Balances reuse/read cost against storage/operations/freshness, local speed against shared-service cost and outage impact, and cached availability against source capacity. Explicitly supports bypass for critical decisions and rejection when caching has no reuse benefit.

evidence.quote: If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.

clarity.reason: Plain actor/state descriptions and short definitions explain hit/miss, key, invalidation, TTL, eviction, coalescing and hit ratio. Examples clarify distinct mechanisms without unnecessary recurring setup or advanced protocol demands.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the data every minute; a later miss must load it again.

outcomes.reason: Transfers reuse/latency benefit to the provided 80/2 ms setting, includes station and language in key, traces application-owned hit and miss/fill, and retains database plus extra-cache costs. All five criteria and exact evidence checked.

Correct old-hours result and delayed old refill after deletion; rejects post-writer freshness guarantee and bypasses the cache for authoritative reads. All four criteria supported; no invented race-fixing protocol.

Correct stale hit at 12:03, expired miss at 12:11 and early-eviction miss at 12:05. Distinguishes lifetime from freshness/residence and neither removal mechanism refreshes data. All four criteria supported.

Chooses shared entry under no-concurrent-fill assumption; explains surviving three local copies, in-process versus network access, shared cost and all-client cache-access loss versus one local loss. Does not infer application failure or automatic source synchronization. All five criteria supported.

Explains simultaneous duplicate misses and one shared in-progress lookup; calculates 20-fold outage overload from supplied facts and caps total fallback with temporary errors. Optional stale use is conditional on independently accessible state and 60-second allowance; main cap/error solution does not depend on a nonexistent reachable old cache. All five criteria satisfied.

Rejects fill-after-single-read cache because no future reuse, cites ample latency/capacity headroom and extra writes/storage/management, and reconsiders repeated expensive or capacity-stressing reads with freshness requirements. All five criteria supported.

sourceChecks.claim: Microsoft caching guidance supports reuse, latency/load benefits and copying/management costs; database authority is explicitly the lesson scenario, not a universal property of every cache product.
Cache-aside source names application lookup, source fetch, fill and response, and warns cached data may differ from source. Hit/miss diagram matches.
Guidance supports keyspace design and private/shared cache access; distinct input-dependent answers logically require distinct identity, and private-result reuse must respect access boundaries.

Source supports store-then-invalidate and explicitly denies consistency guarantees. Delayed-reader counterexample is a valid interleaving of those stated separate operations; authoritative checkout validation avoids trusting stale price.

Redis eviction documents LRU and noeviction behavior. https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/expire/ and Microsoft expiration guidance verify per-entry lifetime, not scheduled refresh; source-data age is a separate quantity.
AWS primary article contrasts on-box/external caching and cold/unavailable dependency consequences; Microsoft private/shared definitions also verify copy independence and network access.
AWS explicitly describes downstream overload from cold/unavailable caches and request coalescing. Source-work caps/rejection follow the stated finite capacity; stale serving remains policy-bound.
Microsoft guidance identifies repeated slow/static/contended reads as good candidates; measurements and low-reuse rejection are correctly conditional. No benchmark or universal improvement asserted.
